title: the fourth floor walk-up Rising
premise: Freya Montrose has spent three years as the night librarian of a sleepless city, orbiting her found family in a fourth-floor walk-up while never quite telling them—or herself—what she actually wants. When the house she grew up in goes to auction, her estranged brother's return drags every buried secret into the open: why Freya left, what their mother hid in the attic, and who really kept the family from falling apart. As the sale deadline closes in, Freya must finally ask the question the whole household arranged itself around—whether belonging can be chosen rather than inherited—and risk losing everyone either way. The novel ends with the house sold, but Freya claiming the walk-up and its people as home, having said the unsayable at last.
about_author: P. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who wrote this debut on breaks between cataloguing other people's letters. They live above a laundromat in a city that never fully sleeps.

chapters.title: The Hours Between
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A night shift at the Meridian Library introduces her quiet rituals: shelving, tea with security guard Odile, and the walk-up family she returns to at dawn. Beat: contentment shadowed by avoidance—we see how carefully Freya practices not saying things.

chapters.title: Fourth Floor, No Elevator
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Portrait of the walk-up household: Theo the insomniac composer, Marisol the hospice nurse, young Dev who sleeps on the couch 'temporarily' for two years. Beat: warmth established; the found family is real but built on everything left unspoken.

chapters.title: Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A certified letter arrives: 14 Larkspur Row goes to auction in six weeks. Freya's hands shake over her tea. Beat: dread—the past arriving with paperwork, demanding an answer she has dodged for fifteen years.

chapters.title: What Dev Saw
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev finds the letter and reads it before Freya can hide it, learning there is a brother named Callum and a mother Freya never mentions. Beat: curiosity curdling into hurt—the family that shares everything has a locked room in it.

chapters.title: The Brother, Arriving
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Callum appears at the library at 3 a.m., older, softer, carrying their mother's boxed papers. He needs Freya to co-sign the estate inventory or the auction proceeds vanish into probate. Beat: collision—the past standing at her desk under fluorescent light.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Childhood
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Sifting the house with Freya, Callum catalogs objects and grievances alike: the piano, the locked attic, the year Freya stopped speaking at dinner. Beat: bitter tenderness—two siblings fluent only in blame rediscovering shared language.

chapters.title: Marisol's Rule
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts Freya about the letter, invoking the walk-up's one rule: no one carries something alone. Freya deflects; Marisol reveals she once did the same and lost someone to it. Beat: warning shot—silence has a body count.

chapters.title: Theo's Nocturne
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, unable to finish his symphony's final movement, recognizes his own blockage in Freya's. He plays her the unfinished pages; she almost tells him everything, then doesn't. Beat: mirrored longing—two artists circling the same unfinished sentence.

chapters.title: The Attic Key
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Callum produces the attic key from their mother's papers. Inside: letters revealing their mother had been quietly paying off their father's debts for years—and a deed amendment naming Freya sole heir. Beat: vertigo—the family's whole architecture was arranged around a secret Freya never knew she held.

chapters.title: Why I Left
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, flashback braided with present. The truth surfaces: Freya discovered the debt at nineteen and left to protect Callum from it, letting him believe she abandoned them. Beat: devastating reframe—her survival cost her the story of herself.

chapters.title: Probate and Small Wars
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Callum learns he was protected, not abandoned, and rages anyway—at Freya, at their mother, at being managed by love. He threatens to contest the deed just to force a conversation. Beat: anger as grief wearing armor.

chapters.title: Dev Runs
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Feeling like a placeholder in everyone's life, Dev takes the auction news as proof that homes are temporary and disappears for three days. Beat: fear rippling outward—one person's flight exposes how fragile the chosen family's covenant is.

chapters.title: The Search Party
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The walk-up mobilizes: Odile checks transit cameras, Theo combs music venues, Marisol works her hospital network. Freya realizes Dev learned disappearing from her. Beat: guilt sharpened into resolve—she will not let Dev inherit her escape route.

chapters.title: Larkspur Row, After Dark
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya finds Dev sitting on the old front steps of 14 Larkspur Row. In the dark house, she tells Dev the truth about why she left—the first full telling out loud. Beat: breakthrough—saying it once makes saying it possible.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile, the walk-up's quiet witness, tells Freya she has watched three years of 'almost' and hands Freya a note Freya once wrote and threw away: the question itself, drafted and abandoned. Beat: confrontation with self—the question was always written; only the asking was missing.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At a household dinner, Freya asks it plainly: if the house sells and the money divides them, do we choose each other anyway—or were we only ever convenient? Silence, then Marisol says yes first. Beat: climax of feeling—the arrangement exposed, and answered.

chapters.title: Bidding War
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Auction day: a developer drives the price up. Callum, now understanding Freya's sacrifice, secretly bids to keep the house—not for himself but to give Freya back her choice. Beat: reversal—the brother becomes the protector.

chapters.title: Sold
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The house sells to strangers. Freya feels neither triumph nor ruin but something stranger: release. She and Callum split the proceeds per their mother's letters, which also name the walk-up tenants as beneficiaries. Beat: grief and grace entangled—the inheritance was never the building.

chapters.title: What We Kept
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Moving day at Larkspur Row: the piano goes to Theo, the letters divided, the attic key retired to a shelf in the Meridian Library. Beat: ceremonial mourning—a good ending honored properly.

chapters.title: Said Aloud
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya finishes the sentence she has practiced for three years—to Theo, to Marisol, to Dev, to Callum, one by one: that they are her family, chosen and permanent. Each answers in kind. Beat: resolution of the central silence—the art of almost ends.

chapters.title: Final Movement
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo completes the symphony's last movement and plays it in the walk-up stairwell, all five of them crowded on the landings. Beat: joy earned—the unfinished thing finished, together.

chapters.title: The Fifth Floor
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, coda. One year later: the walk-up gains a new tenant, a frightened kid Dev brings home. Freya leaves the door unlocked and the kettle filled. Beat: belonging renewed as practice, not possession—the price of survival, paid forward.
